column2: A backstage dressing room before a performance
column3: Lights shine round the big mirror. Red shoes stand under a chair, and a long blue dress hangs by the door. The room smells of flowers and soap. Ella sits very still. A woman paints her lips red. Outside, people laugh and talk. Ella looks at her face in the mirror. Her smile is small, but it is there.
column4: Someone knocks, and every face turns towards the door. Five minutes. The little room is full of coats, bags and bright clothes. Under the warm lights, my brother is fixing his hair for the third time. A cup shakes gently in his hand. From beyond the wall comes the low sound of the audience, like a sea we cannot see.
column5: Powder floated through the dressing room whenever anyone closed a bag. Around the mirrors, bare bulbs warmed our faces while the floor stayed cold beneath our feet. A row of borrowed jackets hung from a pipe. Beside me, Sam whispered his opening words into a folded towel. Then the music began outside. He put the towel down and straightened his shoulders.
column6: Six faces crowded the mirror, though the room held only three performers. Under the bulbs, their painted smiles appeared unusually fixed. Somebody's phone vibrated among the hairpins; nobody reached for it. Through the thin wall came a burst of applause for the previous act. For a moment, all three stood listening, their elaborate costumes rustling whenever they took a breath.
column7: In the interval before the overture, the dressing room seemed to hold its breath. Sequins caught the naked light; a curling iron ticked as it cooled. At the far mirror, an actor inspected a loose thread with extravagant concentration. Everything necessary for becoming somebody else lay within reach. Yet the hands resting on the crowded counter remained unmistakably, vulnerably his own.

column2: A city street during a power cut
column3: The street is dark, but our neighbours are outside. Mr Lee has a little light. It makes a yellow circle on the road. A child holds her mother's hand and looks up. There are stars above the tall buildings. We do not see them on most nights. Someone brings chairs from a shop, and we sit together in the warm air.
column4: When the lights went out, the street changed. The bright shop windows became black mirrors, and the music stopped. For a few seconds, everyone stood still. Then a woman opened her door with a candle in her hand. Soon, small flames shone along the road. Without the noise from the shops, we could hear water running under the drain covers.
column5: Halfway through the evening, the city lost its familiar colours. Shop signs disappeared, leaving dark shapes above the pavement. Cars crawled towards a silent crossroads, their drivers waving one another through. Outside the bakery, people gathered around a battery radio. Its thin music floated between the buildings while the baker handed out warm bread that he could no longer sell.
column6: With the traffic lights dead, the junction acquired a hesitant courtesy. Drivers edged forward, paused, exchanged gestures through open windows. Above them, office blocks had become enormous silhouettes. The smell of fried onions travelled from a stall lit by a camping lamp, drawing a small, patient crowd. A bus passed, briefly lending the pavement the borrowed daylight of its windows.
column7: Deprived of its illuminated promises, the shopping street revealed an older shape: narrow upper windows, uneven cornices, a faded name painted above a modern bank. Candles appeared behind glass. Somewhere, an alarm exhausted itself and fell silent. Only then did the conversation outside the flats become audible, spreading from doorway to doorway with the unhurried warmth of people unexpectedly released from separate rooms.

column2: A frozen pond beneath a pale winter sky
column3: White grass grows round the pond. Ice covers its water, and the sky above is almost white too. A brown leaf sits in the middle. The wind comes, but the leaf does not move. Near my feet, a small bird jumps through the grass. Its feet make little marks in the snow. All around us, the trees are still.
column4: We stopped beside the frozen pond. Snow lay on the wooden seat, and the tall grass wore white coats of ice. Under the pale sky, the pond looked like a large, dirty mirror. A few leaves lay just below its surface. I could see each brown line clearly. Behind us, a dog shook its wet coat. Cold drops hit my boots.
column5: Across the pond, winter had drawn a white line around every reed. The ice was cloudy near the bank but clearer in the middle, where a trapped branch stretched beneath it like a dark hand. Nothing stirred under the pale sky. Then a crow landed on the fence, breaking the stillness with one rough call that seemed much too loud.
column6: A skin of ice concealed the pond's familiar brown water. Bubbles hung beneath it in long, uneven necklaces, and the reeds cast shadows so faint they seemed unfinished. Overhead, the sky offered little distinction between cloud and light. I stood at the bank, listening. Somewhere within the frozen surface, a deep note sounded, then travelled away beneath the snow.
column7: Under a sky bleached almost colourless, the pond resembled an image slowly fading from a photograph. Only the reeds retained their fine brown insistence. Beneath the opaque rim, a chain of bubbles recorded the last movements of water before the freeze. Nothing now disturbed that interrupted passage. Even the wind, dragging loose snow across the surface, left the buried shapes intact.

column2: A greenhouse filled with unfamiliar plants
column3: Inside the glass house, the air is warm and wet. Water falls from a big leaf onto my arm. Some leaves are larger than my head. Others are small and round, like green coins. A red flower hangs over the path. I bend down to look inside it. There is a tiny pool of water at the bottom.
column4: My glasses became wet as soon as I stepped inside. Plants filled every space in the greenhouse. One had long purple leaves; another wore a coat of soft white hair. Above the path hung a flower as big as a plate. Its sweet smell followed me between the tables. Every label had a name I could not say.
column5: Heat closed around us at the greenhouse door. Under the roof, enormous leaves overlapped like umbrellas, catching drops that fell from the misting pipes. I brushed against a plant with stiff silver hairs. Beside it, a green cup held several drowned flies. The flowers were stranger still: spotted, twisted, almost animal. Each turn of the path revealed a different shape.
column6: In the far corner, a flower the colour of raw meat leaned over the path. Its heavy smell drove me towards a neighbouring bed, where tiny white blossoms released something sharp and lemony. Here, beauty refused to follow familiar rules. Leaves resembled pebbles; stems bulged like bottles. Condensation crept down the glass, blurring the ordinary winter garden beyond it.
column7: What appeared at first to be a collection of curiosities gradually resolved into competing strategies for survival. Waxy leaves hoarded moisture; delicate tendrils explored the wire supports with blind persistence. From a hanging basket descended a flower so elaborately folded that it resembled an unfinished thought. Beneath it, the gardener swept fallen petals into a heap, reducing all this extravagance to a morning chore.

column2: A lighthouse on an isolated island
column3: Our boat is small beside the island. High above us stands a tall white tower. Its light moves across the dark water. There is one little house and a wall of grey rocks. A bird calls into the wind. At the top of the tower, a window shines yellow. Someone is awake up there, far from every town.
column4: The lighthouse stood at the island's highest point. Below it, waves broke against black rocks, and white water flew into the air. There were no other buildings except a low stone house. A washing line hung beside its door, but nothing was drying there today. The wind pulled at my coat as I followed the narrow steps up from the boat.
column5: By evening, the lighthouse was the island's only moving light. Its beam swept over wet rocks, vanished across the sea, then returned to find the same small garden and empty landing place. Inside the keeper's kitchen, a kettle clicked off. The sudden quiet made the waves sound nearer. Salt had gathered along the window frame in a thin white crust.
column6: Climbing the spiral staircase, I felt the tower receive each wave through its stone foundations. The vibration rose through the handrail into my fingers. Above, the great lens turned with an almost domestic hum. Beyond the glass, darkness extended in every direction. At regular intervals, the beam revealed a wedge of empty sea, then surrendered it to the night again.
column7: From the mainland, the lighthouse had seemed a single confident stroke against the horizon. Up close, it was a record of maintenance: fresh paint over old cracks, brass polished against salt, a door swollen by successive winters. Around it, the island offered little shelter. Yet in the keeper's window, a pot of basil leaned towards the light with the innocent certainty of a kitchen anywhere.

column2: A scrapyard on the edge of town
column3: Old cars stand in long rows behind the town. Some have no doors, and grass grows through their wheels. A green bus sits by the fence. Its windows are broken, but its big front lights are still there. They look like tired eyes. In the small office, a man drinks tea. Outside his door, a black cat sleeps on a seat.
column4: Beyond the last houses, the scrapyard covered a wide piece of land. Old washing machines stood beside a mountain of bicycle wheels. Rain filled the seats of cars without roofs. Somewhere behind them, a worker dropped a metal pipe. Clang! Birds flew from the fence. Then the yard was quiet again, except for the slow drip of water from a bus.
column5: The gate opened onto a landscape of things that no longer worked. Cars leaned together in uneven towers; a fridge lay on its back, open to the rain. Between them grew bright yellow flowers. I followed the owner past a heap of twisted pipes. He knew where everything was, even the tiny door handle he had promised to find.
column6: At closing time, sunlight caught the scrapyard's broken edges. Shattered windscreens glittered among dull panels, and a line of washing machines faced west like spectators waiting for a show. From the workshop came the sharp scent of cut metal. Beyond the fence, new houses stood in careful rows, their windows reflecting the same copper sky as the ruined cars.
column7: The yard rearranged the town's discarded ambitions into rough categories: engines, appliances, the ornamental ironwork of demolished balconies. Among these heaps, a crane moved with surprising delicacy, selecting a crushed car and lowering it onto the scales. Its tyres had disappeared; its registration plate remained legible. For a moment, the familiar arrangement of letters made the anonymous wreck seem awkwardly personal.

column2: A settlement built among the branches of enormous trees
column3: Our houses are high in the trees. Wooden paths go from door to door, and leaves grow beside the windows. From my bed, I can see birds in their nests. Below us, the forest is dark and green. Mum calls from the next house. Lunch is ready. I cross the little bridge, with the smell of warm bread in the air.
column4: The village moved gently when the wind blew. Houses rested between thick branches, and rope bridges joined their little gardens. A boy carried a basket of washing past my window. Far below his feet, clouds of white mist hid the ground. From a nearby kitchen came the sound of plates. Even up here, somebody was late for dinner.
column5: Morning reached the highest homes first. Their windows flashed between the leaves while the lower walkways remained in shadow. I followed a woman carrying water across a bridge that swayed beneath our steps. Beneath us lay another world of branches, ladders and drifting mist. Above, a child leaned from a doorway to lower a basket to the baker.
column6: Built into the forks of enormous trees, the settlement adjusted itself to the forest's movement. Bridges sagged and tightened; hanging lamps traced small circles in the dusk. Through an open doorway, I glimpsed a family clearing supper from a table fitted around a living trunk. The bark continued through the ceiling. Somewhere above their roof, an unseen bird began to sing.
column7: The oldest houses bore evidence of negotiation with their hosts. A root had lifted a doorstep; a thickening branch had been granted its own opening in a wall. Nothing here could be built and simply forgotten. On the communal platform, carpenters discussed a split beam while children skipped around the tree's broad trunk, accommodating its presence without the slightest sense of inconvenience.

column2: A skatepark on a warm evening
column3: The park is still warm in the evening sun. Wheels roll over the grey ground. Click, clack! A boy jumps with his board, and his friends shout. Near the wall, a girl tries a small jump again. Her face is hot and red. This time, she stays on the board. Her brother claps, and she gives him a big smile.
column4: Long shadows stretched across the skatepark. The concrete was warm through my jeans as I sat beside the ramp. Boards rattled past, followed by laughter and the soft sound of rubber shoes. A girl in a yellow shirt waited at the top. For a moment, she was still against the pink sky. Then she bent her knees and rolled down.
column5: By seven, the heat had begun to leave the concrete. Skaters took turns beneath the long evening shadows, their wheels humming until a jump broke the rhythm. Clack. A cheer. Another try. Near the fence, two beginners practised the same small turn. Nobody hurried them. The older skaters rested on their boards, sharing water and watching the light fade.
column6: From the highest ramp, the skatepark resembled a shallow grey sea, its waves fixed in concrete. Riders dropped into the curves and rose again, briefly outlined against the evening sky. Dust lifted whenever a board landed badly. At the edge, a boy rehearsed a movement with his hands, explaining a trick to his sister while she studied the slope.
column7: Evening loosened the skatepark's competitive energy. Between attempts, riders lingered in the last broad patch of sunlight, comparing bruises and replaying successes with increasingly generous gestures. The concrete retained the day's warmth. When a newcomer finally landed a difficult turn, the applause came from several directions at once, briefly gathering this scattered company into something like a team. Then the wheels resumed their separate rhythms.

column2: A space station orbiting an unfamiliar planet
column3: A purple planet fills our big window. White clouds make circles above its dark hills. We do not know their names. Inside the station, small lights shine along the walls. A fan makes a quiet sound. My sister puts her hand on the glass. Far below us, a long green lake catches the sun. It looks like a bright ribbon.
column4: From the station window, the planet looked almost friendly. Blue clouds covered its wide orange seas, and two small moons shone above them. Inside, the air smelled of warm machines and fresh coffee. A green light flashed beside the door. Beyond that door, another team was sleeping. We spoke quietly while the strange new world turned slowly below us.
column5: Our first morning began with a sunrise beneath our feet. Light spilled over the planet's curved edge, revealing storms wider than countries. Inside the station, breakfast trays waited in their usual slots. The ordinary smell of toast seemed strange against that enormous view. I held my cup with both hands and watched a shadow slide across a continent nobody had named.
column6: The observation deck faced the planet's night side. Below, lightning spread through enormous cloud systems, briefly exposing patterns no map recorded. Behind me, the station continued its modest routines: a printer chattering, someone searching for a missing pen. This closeness of the ordinary to the unimaginable was hardest to grasp. On the windowsill, a taped photograph had begun to curl.
column7: Only when the station passed into shadow did the planet disclose its stranger colours. Across the dark hemisphere, violet bands gathered and dissolved, too extensive to be cities, too regular to be easily dismissed. The scientists stood shoulder to shoulder at the glass. Behind them, an unfinished meal cooled beneath the ventilation fans, its small domestic smells absurdly reassuring in the face of such scale.

column2: An overgrown city reclaimed by nature
column3: Trees grow in the middle of the road. Their leaves hide the old street lights, and flowers fill the cracks below. In a shop window, a bird feeds its young. The glass is gone now. A fox walks past a red bus and stops to look at us. Then it runs into the long grass outside the empty school.
column4: We followed the river along the old city road. Green water ran between the pavements, past shops with trees inside them. High above us, flowers grew from a broken office window. Their pink heads moved in the breeze. A road sign still pointed towards the airport, but a thick wall of leaves covered the way. We could hear birds everywhere.
column5: The city was loud with life. Parrots argued from office windows, and insects hummed above the flooded square. Under the trees stood the remains of a bus shelter, its route map pale behind cracked glass. A vine had followed the red line towards the hospital. Beyond it, a young deer stepped carefully through the revolving doors of a department store.
column6: At the former shopping centre, daylight entered through a roof of leaves. Rain had washed soil into the escalators, where ferns now climbed in orderly green ranks. The fountain supported a small pond, busy with insects. I sat beneath a faded advertisement for a tropical holiday and listened to water dripping through the floors, floor after floor, towards the buried car park.
column7: The boulevard's old symmetry remained visible beneath its exuberant new inhabitants. Trees emerged at irregular intervals from the paving, ignoring the empty planting pits the planners had provided. On a bank's stone steps, moss softened the carved assurance of permanence. Farther along, roots had opened the road with patient, muscular pressure. Through that widening seam, a narrow stream carried petals towards the former financial district.

column3: Fish swim past our round window. Some are small and blue. One is long and silver, like a knife. Inside the station, the lights are bright, but the sea outside is dark. My dad sits at a desk and watches a screen. On it, a small crab walks over the sand. Its legs move like tiny busy fingers.
column4: The sea pressed close to every window. Outside, long plants moved slowly above the sandy floor, and a yellow fish watched us through the glass. Our room was small, with two beds and a table fixed to the wall. Water pipes made soft clicking sounds. I put my shoes under the bed and looked out again. The fish was still there.
column5: At night, the research station's windows became pools of light in the dark sea. Tiny creatures gathered outside, rising and falling like dust in a sunbeam. Beyond them, our lamps reached only a few metres. I could hear a scientist washing cups in the next room. Somewhere underneath that familiar clatter ran the steady hum that kept our air moving.
column6: From the dining area, the seabed appeared almost still. Only after several minutes did I notice the sand shifting, grain by grain, beneath a half-buried ray. Above us, a pump started with a shudder, sending ripples across my tea. The station's instruments tracked currents and temperatures continuously. At the window, however, understanding demanded something slower: staying long enough to see.
column7: Beyond the observation glass, a pale arm emerged from the rocks, explored an empty shell and withdrew. The octopus remained almost indistinguishable from its surroundings. Inside, researchers annotated the footage beneath fluorescent lights, assigning times and measurements to the encounter. Outside, the creature altered its colour and slipped away, leaving the instruments to register a patch of seabed that looked, once again, entirely unoccupied.
